editions.intro: The Nvidia scandal’s fallout inside the Trump administration leads both the New York Times and the Washington Post, while the BBC leads with five EU countries’ deportation center in Rwanda (international) and a review of youth unemployment (UK). Robert Pattinson’s casting as the next James Bond is on every front and near the top of most most-read lists.
editions.cover: The New York Times leads with the Trump administration’s split over China chip policy breaking into public view, and the Washington Post with Trump seeing “both sides” as the Nvidia scandal fuels a feud between his top aides. The Guardian’s international front leads with world leaders gathering for the Apec and Asean summits, its UK front with police “retreating from streets.” The BBC leads with an EU deportation center in Rwanda and, in the UK, a youth jobs review; The Times of London leads with a “Farage penalty” in the Brexit reset deal; the Times of Israel’s newest story is an attack near Jericho. Robert Pattinson as James Bond tops the Guardian’s most-read list. Also getting big play: the Grammy nominations, Thursday’s GTA VI release and two Israeli Grammy nominees.

editions.intro: Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s chief executive leads the BBC, the Guardian, ynet and the New York Times this morning. The Washington Post leads with Chris Van Hollen’s challenge to Chuck Schumer, and readers are clicking on a global Microsoft outage and Trump ending Vance’s Iran talks.
editions.cover: Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s chief executive leads the morning: both BBC homepages, both Guardian editions and ynet open with it, and the New York Times opens with Trump having urged Huang to fight for his job, while a Huang biographer’s column tops its trending list. The Washington Post leads with Senator Chris Van Hollen’s challenge to Chuck Schumer. The Times of London leads with six more women accusing Russell Brand, whose prison term tops the BBC most-read list, and the Times of Israel with Netanyahu’s media machine. A global Microsoft outage tops the Guardian’s most-viewed list; Trump ending Vance’s Iran talks tops the Post’s. Away from the news, Johnny Depp’s “Ebenezer” is widely reviewed, Duran Duran’s drummer quits, and Harry Kane scores on his record 126th England cap.

editions.cover: Nvidia leads the morning: the New York Times and both BBC homepages open with its board weighing the future of chief executive Jensen Huang, after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a relationship with an executive who reports to him. A live page on a deadly Brooklyn building collapse sits at the top of the NYT homepage and is No. 1 on its trending list. The Washington Post leads with Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate win in Mississippi, which also tops the Guardian’s most-viewed list, while Pete Hegseth being scolded at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is No. 1 on the Post’s most-read list. The Guardian’s UK edition still leads with the David Walliams fallout, and the Times of Israel’s newest item is Hezbollah’s leader on the elections. Away from the news, Pochettino is set to take over Manchester United, Dua Lipa will headline Coachella, and Israeli outlets review the new season of “HaTabach.”

editions.cover: The big newsrooms split on what matters most today. The New York Times leads with the woman at the center of the Nvidia spy scandal, which is also No. 1 on the Times and Washington Post most-read lists. The Post leads with House Republicans blocking the Hegseth impeachment. In Britain, The Guardian and The Times lead with the allegations against David Walliams, which he denies, and the BBC's top stories include the arrest of a US Army soldier near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia. The Times of Israel leads with Netanyahu's Knesset speech. Away from the news pages, M John Harrison became the first science fiction author to win the Booker Prize, Stacy Keach died at 85, and Paul McCartney became a billionaire.
